abstract: All-optical control of magnetization via the Inverse Faraday Effect presents a transformative pathway for ultrafast high-density data storage and nanoscale spintronics. However, unlocking its full potential requires moving beyond traditional gold-centric, narrowband constraints. In this study, we present a comprehensive theoretical framework evaluating IFE-driven static magnetic field generation across a diverse library of plasmonic materials, including gold, silver, copper, aluminum, and titanium nitride. Using a dimensionally tunable coaxial nanoantenna, we map the optomagnetic response across the deep-ultraviolet to near-infrared spectrum. Our findings reveal highly distinct, material-dependent behaviors: aluminum uniquely sustains robust magnetization in the deep-UV, whereas silver, copper, and gold exhibit superior efficiency at longer wavelengths. Crucially, we demonstrate that shifting the excitation to the near-infrared regime amplifies the generated magnetic field by several orders of magnitude, establishing these frequencies as critical for helicity-dependent all-optical switching. Furthermore, by resolving the local optical spin density, we elucidate how extreme subwavelength confinement drives synchronized drift currents, enabling efficient multispectral magnetization through localized surface plasmon resonances and higher-order Fabry-Perot modes. Strikingly, comparing these distinct modes reveals that structural geometry tunes the resonant wavelength, while the maximum achievable optomagnetic amplitude is fundamentally governed by the metal's intrinsic properties.
